Covetous means having a strong, greedy desire to possess something that belongs to someone else. It describes a person who looks at what others have — their money, their success, their belongings, their relationships — and deeply, almost hungrily, wants it for themselves.

The key word here is someone else's. You are not just wishing for something nice in general. You are specifically eyeing what another person already has and wanting to take it, own it, or have it instead of them.

Imagine your neighbor parks a brand new car in their driveway. You don't just think, "Oh, that's a nice car." Instead, you feel a deep, burning desire — almost an ache — to have that specific car, or at least one exactly like it. You keep thinking about it. You resent that they have it and you don't. That feeling is what covetous describes.

Now scale that up to wealth, status, a job, a partner, fame, or talent — and you have the full picture.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

Covetous is not a neutral word. It carries a negative moral weight. When you call someone covetous, you are not simply saying they want nice things. You are saying:

  • Their desire is excessive — beyond normal wanting.
  • Their desire is self-centered — it's about having what others have, not about genuine need.
  • Their desire often comes with resentment or envy toward the person who has the thing they want.
  • They may be unwilling to be satisfied with what they already have.

It implies a character flaw — a kind of spiritual or moral greed that goes beyond just being ambitious or aspirational.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are close in meaning but not identical:

  • Greedy = wanting more of something (money, food, power) in a general, excessive way. A greedy person just wants more. They may not care specifically what others have.
  • Envious = feeling unhappy or bitter because someone else has something you want. It's mostly an emotion — a feeling of resentment.
  • Jealous = fearing you'll lose something (or someone) you already have to another person. Jealousy is about protecting what's yours.
  • Covetous = specifically and intensely desiring to possess what someone else has. It combines greed and envy and adds a sharp focus on the other person's possessions.

So covetous is more targeted than greedy, more desire-driven than envious, and unlike jealousy, it's about wanting to gain, not to protect.

Covetous is not a mild word. It suggests a persistent, consuming desire — not a passing thought like "I wish I had that." It's the kind of wanting that lingers, that colors how you see others, and that can quietly poison your contentment with your own life. A covetous person is rarely at peace because they are always measuring what they have against what someone else has.

• She cast a covetous eye on her colleague's promotion, even though she hadn't worked as hard.
  • His covetous nature made it impossible for him to enjoy his own success — he was always fixated on what others had achieved.
  • The merchant gave a covetous glance at the rare jewel in the trader's hand.
  • Growing up in poverty made him covetous of the comfortable lives he saw around him.
  • She wasn't simply ambitious — she was covetous, wanting not just success but the exact life her sister had built.

• Covetously (adverb) — in a covetous manner. "He stared covetously at the painting."
  • Covetousness (noun) — the state or quality of being covetous. "His covetousness drove a wedge between him and his friends."
  • Covet (verb) — the action. "She coveted her friend's talent."
What Kind of People or Situations Is This Word Used For?

Covetous is most often used to describe:

  • A person who is obsessed with wealth or material things they don't own.
  • Someone who resents another person's success, talent, or happiness.
  • A character in literature or storytelling who is driven by greed and desire — often a villain or a morally flawed protagonist.
  • Situations where desire for what's not yours leads to poor decisions or harm.

It appears often in formal writing, literature, religious texts, and moral discussions. In everyday conversation, people might just say "greedy" or "jealous," but covetous captures something more specific and more pointed than either of those words.

Covetous = greedily wanting what belongs to someone else, in a way that is persistent, morally questionable, and often tinged with resentment.

If a person looks at another person's life — their house, their money, their partner, their talent — and feels a deep, burning hunger to have that for themselves, that person is covetous.
